concepts.name: Android framework calls in local unit tests

questions.prompt: An app targeting Android 12 or higher builds `PendingIntent.getActivity(context, 0, intent, 0)` for a notification tap. What happens, and what is the right fix?

choices.text: It works, but Lint warns; add `FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT` to silence the warning
It throws `SecurityException`; mark the target Activity as exported instead
It still works and is mutable by default; add `FLAG_MUTABLE` only for inline replies
It throws `IllegalArgumentException`; pass `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` unless it must change

questions.explanation: Apps targeting Android 12 (API 31) or higher must give every `PendingIntent` a mutability flag; without `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` or `FLAG_MUTABLE` the system throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Prefer `FLAG_IMMUTABLE`, so other apps can't fill in the intent, and use `FLAG_MUTABLE` only when a feature depends on it, such as direct reply or bubbles. Exporting the Activity is unrelated and would widen access.

sources.title: Intents and intent filters | App architecture | Android Developers
sources.claim: Apps targeting Android 12 or higher must specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE for each PendingIntent, or the system throws IllegalArgumentException; use FLAG_IMMUTABLE whenever possible and FLAG_MUTABLE only when functionality depends on it.

sources.title: Pending intents | Security | Android Developers
sources.claim: Specify mutability, for example with FLAG_IMMUTABLE, to prevent unfilled fields from being filled in by a malicious application.

questions.prompt: A Compose UI test must start your real `MainActivity` and read a string with that Activity's `getString()`. Which test rule fits?

choices.text: `createComposeRule()`, because it always starts the app's launcher Activity
`createAndroidComposeRule<MainActivity>()`, which gives you that Activity
`createComposeRule()`, then call `setContent { MainActivity() }` in the test
Only an `ActivityScenarioRule`, because node finders need no Compose rule

questions.explanation: `createComposeRule()` is for tests that don't need an Activity: you supply the content with `setContent {}`. When you need an Activity, its resources or its own content, use `createAndroidComposeRule<YourActivity>()`, which gives you that Activity. The finders and assertions such as `onNodeWithText` come from the Compose test rule, so an `ActivityScenarioRule` alone isn't enough.

sources.title: Test your Compose layout | Jetpack Compose | Android Developers
sources.claim: Use createComposeRule() when you don't need access to an activity and set content with setContent; use createAndroidComposeRule<YourActivity>() when you need access to an activity; ui-test-manifest is needed for createComposeRule() but not for createAndroidComposeRule.

questions.prompt: A local unit test of a formatter fails with `Method ... not mocked` when the code calls an Android framework class. Explain why, and compare the ways to fix it.

model_answer.summary: Local tests run against a stub Android library whose method bodies are removed, so framework calls throw; mocking or Robolectric are the fixes, and `returnDefaultValues` is a last resort.
key_points: Local tests run on the JVM against a mockable Android library: the framework's public classes and methods with their code removed, so calling one throws `Method ... not mocked`
`unitTests.returnDefaultValues = true` makes those methods return null or zero, but it is a last resort: it can hide regressions and let failing tests pass
Prefer mocking the Android dependency (Mockito, MockK) or running the test with Robolectric's shadows of Android classes

questions.explanation: The error is not a bug in the test; it is how local tests protect you from silently calling stubbed framework code. Switching on default values makes the error go away by hiding it, which is why the docs call it a last resort.

sources.title: Build local unit tests | Test your app on Android | Android Developers
sources.claim: The mockable Android library has the framework's public methods with their code removed, so calling one in a local test throws 'Method ... not mocked'; mock the dependency or use Robolectric, and use unitTests.returnDefaultValues only as a last resort, since null/zero values can hide regressions and let failing tests pass.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

choices.text: A notification's content tap that opens one fixed screen of your app
A notification direct-reply action, which adds the typed text to it
A notification action that marks one message read through a receiver
A launcher shortcut that opens your settings screen with fixed extras

questions.explanation: Mutable PendingIntents are only for features that depend on the system or another app changing the intent: a direct reply action adds the reply to its clip data, and bubbles, location updates and `AlarmManager` alarms are other listed cases. The other three fire a fixed intent, so `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` is right and safer.

sources.title: Intents and intent filters | App architecture | Android Developers
sources.claim: Use FLAG_MUTABLE only when functionality depends on it: direct reply actions in notifications (the reply changes the clip data), Android Auto, bubbles, location updates and AlarmManager alarms; otherwise use FLAG_IMMUTABLE.

questions.prompt: When do you choose `createComposeRule()` and when `createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` for a Compose UI test? Say what each gives you and what setup each needs.

model_answer.summary: `createComposeRule()` tests content you set yourself with no Activity of yours; `createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` is for when you need an Activity, and only the first needs the `ui-test-manifest` dependency.
key_points: `createComposeRule()` when you don't need an Activity: you call `setContent {}` with the composable under test, for example a screen given a fake UI state
`createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` when you need access to an Activity, such as its resources or the real Activity's content

questions.explanation: Testing a composable in isolation with fake state is the default, fast option. Reaching for the Activity rule makes sense only when the test really needs the Activity.

sources.title: Test your Compose layout | Jetpack Compose | Android Developers
sources.claim: createComposeRule() is for tests that don't need an activity and uses setContent; createAndroidComposeRule<YourActivity>() is for when you need access to an activity; ui-test-manifest is needed for createComposeRule() but not for createAndroidComposeRule.

questions.prompt: A teammate sets `testOptions.unitTests.isReturnDefaultValues = true` so local tests stop throwing `Method ... not mocked`. What is the risk?

choices.text: Framework calls now run the real code, so results depend on the host computer
Tests now run inside Robolectric, so the whole local suite gets much slower
Framework calls return null or zero, which can hide bugs and pass bad tests
It applies only to instrumented tests, so local tests keep throwing anyway

questions.explanation: With `returnDefaultValues`, the stubbed framework methods return null or zero instead of throwing. Nothing real runs, so a test can pass while the code is wrong, and the regressions that follow are hard to debug. The docs recommend it only as a last resort, after mocking or Robolectric.

sources.title: Build local unit tests | Test your app on Android | Android Developers
sources.claim: unitTests.returnDefaultValues makes stubbed methods return null or zero; these values can introduce regressions that are hard to debug and might allow failing tests to pass, so use it only as a last resort.

questions.prompt: A local unit test of a formatter fails with `Method ... not mocked` when the code calls an Android framework class. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Local tests run against an Android library whose method code is removed
`returnDefaultValues = true` makes those methods run their real code
`returnDefaultValues = true` is a last resort: it can let failing tests pass
The error means this test can only ever run on a real device or an emulator
A Robolectric shadow of the Android class is a better fix than default values

questions.explanation: Local tests run on the JVM against a mockable Android library: the framework's public methods with their code removed, so calling one throws `Method ... not mocked`. `unitTests.returnDefaultValues = true` makes those methods return null or zero, not run real code, and the docs call it a last resort because those values can hide regressions and let failing tests pass. Prefer a test double, such as a fake or a Robolectric shadow of the Android class; moving to an instrumented test is one option, not the only one.

sources.title: Build local unit tests
sources.claim: The mockable Android library throws 'Method ... not mocked' when its methods are called; `unitTests.returnDefaultValues = true` makes them return null or zero instead, which can introduce regressions and let failing tests pass, so use it only as a last resort; prefer test doubles such as fakes or Robolectric shadows.

questions.prompt: You're writing a Compose UI test. Which statements about `createComposeRule()` and `createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `createComposeRule()` suits tests needing no Activity: you call `setContent`
`createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` also needs the `ui-test-manifest` dependency
`createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` suits tests that need access to an Activity
`createComposeRule()` launches your app's main Activity with its real content
`createComposeRule()` needs `ui-test-manifest` as a `debugImplementation`

questions.explanation: `createComposeRule()` is for testing Compose content without an Activity of your own: you call `setContent {}` with the composable under test, such as a screen given a fake UI state. `createAndroidComposeRule<A>()` is for when you need access to an Activity. The `androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-manifest` `debugImplementation` dependency is needed for `createComposeRule()`, but not for `createAndroidComposeRule<A>()`.

sources.title: Test your Compose layout
sources.claim: `createComposeRule()` is used with `setContent` when no activity is needed, and `createAndroidComposeRule<YourActivity>()` when you need access to an activity; `ui-test-manifest` is needed for `createComposeRule()` but not for `createAndroidComposeRule<YourActivity>()`.
